source.title: On Representational Alignment among Embodied Agents

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops a theoretical account of task-relative representational sufficiency in embodied-agent hand-off scenarios. It does not test neural-network convergence, alignment across model scale or modalities, or similarity measures named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper analytically compares relative synchronization with absolute hand-off timing, but these toy-scenario results are about task-dependent relational sufficiency, not convergence of network representations. No neural models, representation-distance metrics, scaling sweep, or cross-modal paired-data alignment are tested. Cited alignment methods are background rather than results of this study.
record.test_reason: The paper is purely theoretical. It analyzes toy hand-off scenarios in which two embodied agents compare hand-specified estimates of event time. No neural networks, learned representations, similarity measures, model-scale sweeps or cross-modal data appear. It argues that global alignment may be unnecessary for a task, but never measures whether representations converge. Relative representations (Moschella et al.) and sheaf-based alignment are cited as background only. None of V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that alignment between embodied agents need only proceed until the remaining ambiguity cannot change the task-relevant outcome. In their analytical example, relative synchronization needs zero extra scalar anchors and absolute timing needs one for exact response sufficiency. They add that adequacy can need even less information: a Boolean window cue suffices without reconstructing the response.
record.recipe_differences: The paper presents a theoretical relational-sufficiency framework and analytical toy scenarios, not a representation-similarity or convergence method.
record.method_sensitivity: The analytical outcome changes with the task: relative synchronization requires no additional anchor, whereas absolute hand-off timing requires one.

fits_no_version.finding: In two analytically solved hand-off scenarios, the agents' relational evidence (the difference of their time estimates) leaves the same common-shift ambiguity. That ambiguity needs no extra anchor for relative synchronization, but one scalar anchor for absolute hand-off timing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How much representational alignment embodied agents need is task-relative: residual disagreement need not be resolved when the interaction is invariant to it.

record.problems: The evidence is theoretical and based on analytically solvable toy scenarios, not empirical or simulated robot experiments. The paper notes that its results assume a defined transport and fixed interaction, and that the local anchor bound does not establish global sufficiency.

untested.parts: All of it: no models, no scale or capability variation, no similarity measurement.
All of it: no vision or language models and no paired image–caption data.
All of it: no networks trained from different seeds.
All of it: representational transport is assumed to exist, not learned or evaluated; no mapping-loss, stitching or relative-representation results.
All of it: no features, neurons, SAE features or circuits.
All of it: no similarity metric, metric settings or input/OOD variation.
All of it: no measured alignment level, plateau, or test of shared data/objectives as causes.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T6 is correct. The term 'representational alignment' here means agents' hand-specified state estimates, not learned neural representations; this should not be read as evidence on the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. The paper does not cite either original source. The authors state that empirical and robot experiments are left for future work.

versions.untested_parts: Not tested: model scale or capability, independent model training, architecture/objective/data variation, or representational-distance convergence.
Not tested: vision-language models, paired images and captions, or alignment as model performance changes.
Not tested: networks trained from different seeds, shared features, or subspaces.
Representational transport is assumed in the framework; the paper does not test mapping quality, loss, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping.
Not tested: recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
Not tested: convergence metrics, metric settings, input dependence, or out-of-distribution effects.
The paper does not measure convergence, plateaus, shared training data or objectives, or whether representations encode a common model of reality.

rows.subject: S1-R
rows.operation_detail: Analytically evaluates relational sufficiency for relative synchronization.
rows.measure: Minimum additional scalar anchors for response sufficiency
rows.note: The common-mode ambiguity is task-invariant in this scenario, so the paper derives that no additional anchor is required.
rows.check: This is an analytical derivation (m_min = 0 for S1-R) about anchor counts for hand-specified time estimates, not representation convergence. The 'observed' state has no meaning against any version; the link to none is correct.

rows.subject: S1-A
rows.operation_detail: Analytically evaluates relational sufficiency for absolute hand-off timing.
rows.measure: Minimum additional scalar anchors for exact response sufficiency
rows.note: The same common-mode ambiguity affects the task-relevant response here; the paper derives that one scalar anchor is required.
rows.check: This is an analytical derivation (m_min = 1 for S1-A, exact response sufficiency), not a measure of representational similarity between models. The link to none is correct.
